patch.value: Reads emit ids one per line, bulk writes accept them only comma-joined in argv, and a bulk write that matched nothing exits 0

Every read surface in pm emits item ids one per line once an agent has piped it through jq. Every bulk mutation surface accepts ids only as one comma-joined string in argv. Nothing in the product bridges the two, the established stdin convention is not honored on the selector, and a request that matched nothing still exits 0, so the failure is invisible to the shell operator that scripts actually branch on.

Measured live on 2026-08-01 at 2026.8.1 in an isolated sandbox with PM_GLOBAL_PATH outside the repository and PM_NO_TELEMETRY set:

1. Transport. update-many --ids - and update-many --ids @ids.txt both parse the literal token as an id. The dash is an established stdin convention on this CLI, honored by --comment, --note, --learning, --dep and --file, and by append --body. It is not honored by the id selector, so the natural pipeline of read into jq into mutate cannot be written. The workaround is shell interpolation of a comma-joined string, which places the whole selection inside argv. ARG_MAX on this host is 2,097,152 bytes; at eight bytes per id that caps a single bulk mutation at roughly 260,000 items, and every one of those bytes is also a token if an agent constructs the list itself.

2. Sibling divergence. update-many reports unmatched ids correctly, in both the default encoding and json, as unmatched_ids and unmatched_count. That behavior shipped for closed item pm-ukml. close-many, the sibling that shares the whole filter grammar, reports neither key in either encoding: close-many --ids pm-zzzz9 --reason probe --dry-run --json returns matched_count 0, item_plans [], ids [], and no unmatched field at all. The fix landed on one of the two commands that had the defect.

3. Exit contract. update-many --ids pm-zzzz9,pm-yyyy8 --add-tags probe exits 0. close-many --ids pm-zzzz9 --reason probe exits 0. A partially matched request, one real id and one bogus, also exits 0 with matched_count 1 and unmatched_count 1. In a pipeline the only signal available without re-parsing json is the exit code, and it says success for a mutation that changed nothing.

Together these three make the round trip between a read and a write non-composable at exactly the scale the product is aimed at. The user-facing requirement is that pm compose with grep and jq to build queries and mutations on the fly; today the read half composes and the write half does not.

Scope fence. This is the id selector transport and its miss semantics. It is not the file-valued flag stdin convention (pm-iktj, whose acceptance criteria are scoped to file-reading flags and therefore exclude --ids). It is not the batch json mutation surface (closed pm-xm7c). It is not the explicit id filter itself (closed pm-1h99) nor the unmatched reporting that shipped for update-many (closed pm-ukml); the close-many half of that same defect is the escape this item carries, which is why the escape ratchet is cited.

Proposed resolution: accept - and @path on --ids across every bulk selector so a newline-delimited id stream is a first-class input; make close-many report unmatched ids identically to update-many in both encodings; and give the family one declared miss policy with a non-zero exit when a request matched nothing, with the tolerant behavior available behind an explicit flag rather than as the default.

--ids accepts - to read a newline or comma delimited id stream from stdin, and @path to read the same from a file, on every bulk selector that declares --ids; close-many reports unmatched_ids and unmatched_count in both the default encoding and json, matching update-many exactly; A bulk mutation whose matched_count is zero while unmatched_count is greater than zero exits non-zero, with the tolerant behavior reachable only through an explicit opt-in flag; The declared miss policy is identical across update-many and close-many and is stated once in the scripting contract; A regression test pipes ids from a read command through jq into a bulk mutation and asserts the mutation applied, with a negative control asserting the non-zero exit on a total miss
